source_title: VisionQuest Just Brought Back The One MCU Villain We Never Thought We'd See Again
source_excerpt:
One of the great things about the immortality of the MCU is that fans can be reassured that, as long as they are patient enough, every forgotten character will come back eventually. The Incredible Hulk 's Samuel Sterns finally returned in Captain America: Brave New World, the Defenders are reuniting in Daredevil: Born Again Season 3, and VisionQuest has at last resurrected Ultron, 11 years after his one-and-done appearance in Avengers: Age of Ultron .
James Spader's comeback as the sassiest evil robot around has grabbed most of the attention, but he's actually not the only villain we haven't seen for a while who makes an appearance on the show. VisionQuest Episode 6, "Deadlock," sees the Vision and his estranged son Tommy travel to Madripoor — itself a returning bit of MCU lore, as the crime-soaked city was introduced in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier — where they end up joining forces with Paladin against a common enemy, one who should be familiar to long-term Marvel fans.
The MCU's Very First Villain Returns After 18 Years in VisionQuest
Earlier episodes established that the Paladin's mystery client had canceled his contract to capture Vision in response to his prior failure. However, the bounty hunter's professional pride wouldn't let him give up the chase. In "Deadlock," Paladin tracks the synthezoid down to Madripoor, but their face-off is interrupted by an agent of the Ten Rings organization, who has been hired to apprehend the Vision in Paladin's place. It's Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar, not seen since 2008's Iron Man .
As played by Faran Tahir, Raza has the honor of being the MCU's very first villain. He is the main antagonist of the first half of Iron Man , as it is he who kidnaps Tony Stark in Afghanistan. Later on, it is revealed he was hired to do this by Tony's treacherous partner, Obadiah Stane. The whole plan, of course, backfired when Tony rose up to become Iron Man and opposed the Ten Rings, diminishing the organization's power and influence in the Middle East.
18 years later, Raza is back, and he's had something of a makeover. In VisionQuest , the villain sports a more urban look, swapping his sand-dusted military fatigues for a sharp dark suit. While taunting him, Paladin mentions that the last he heard of Raza, he was rotting in a Ten Rings prison. This suggests Raza was punished for his mishandling of the Tony Stark situation and is perhaps a freelance mercenary at this point.
Alternatively, he may have been re-employed by the Ten Rings after the syndicate underwent a regime change. In Shang-Chi and the Ten Rings , Xu Wenwu — the real Mandarin whom both Trevor Slattery and Aldrich Killian impersonated — died and his daughter, Xialing, took his place as the Ten Rings' leader. Fans have been wondering when the Ten Rings would reappear ever since, given the way development on Shang-Chi 2 has stalled .
Raza's return is long overdue as Tahir has previously revealed that he was supposed to appear in all three movies of the Iron Man trilogy, before Marvel evolved their plans for the films and eliminated his character entirely. Showrunner Terry Matalas was inspired to bring the actor back for VisionQuest after working with Tahir on his Syfy series, 12 Monkeys (which also starred Paladin actor Todd Stashwick and E.D.I.T.H. actress Emily Hampshire).
VisionQuest Is the Latest MCU Project to Explore Tony Stark's Dark Legacy
What's interesting about the return of Raza is that it is just one of many ways in which VisionQuest calls back to Iron Man's MCU history. Not only do you have Ultron and Vision, two AIs who consider Tony something of a father figure, but F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady) is also a major character, one who has displayed PTSD from Stark's death in Avengers: Endgame . Speaking of which, James D'Arcy also reprised his role as Jarvis from Endgame (and Agent Carter ).
What's more, the series has introduced a new AI villain, Jocasta . As played by T'Nia Miller, Jocasta is a digital copy of the consciousness of Josephine Carrington, a brilliant neuroscientist. VisionQuest reveals that it was Carrington who pioneered the development of AI in the Marvel world and not Tony. In fact, Jocasta is now on a murderous rampage to get revenge on Carrington's former colleagues who sold her work to Stark Industries while she was dying from a terminal illness.
In many ways, then, Jocasta is the latest MCU villain who owes their existence to Iron Man . Exploring the dark legacy of the hero has been a preoccupation of the Spider-Man movies, in particular. Brand New Day, for example, revealed the amoral experiments on mutants conducted by the Department of Damage Control — an agency created by Tony himself. Damage Control has also played antagonistic roles in Ms. Marvel and Wonder Man .
Of course, the biggest exploration of Tony's dark legacy may be about to happen in Avengers: Doomsday . It's still unclear whether Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom will be treated as a Stark variant or not, but the Avengers: Endgame Encore re-release certainly heavily hinted at a connection in its end-credits scene. Is the Multiverse Saga's obsession with tarnishing Tony's legacy leading to something big? Or is it simply a sign of changing cultural attitudes? After all, billionaire tech bros with big egos are more controversial figures nowadays than they used to be.
At the very least, the continuing comebacks of characters and concepts from Iron Man's past — like Raza — confirms what was already made clear from Downey's imminent Doomsday return: the current slate of MCU projects seem more than happy to exist in Tony Stark's shadow. Even if that shadow is becoming darker over time.
